rows.speaker: ابن قتيبة
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba cites Dhu al-Rumma’s image of setting stars to support reading dulūk as sunset; an earlier verse associates sunset with the sun’s setting.
rows.anchor: واحتج ابن قتيبة بقول ذي الرمة :

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sunset evidence does not exclude noon: dulūk means inclination or change, which occurs at sunset, while sunset is only one kind of such movement, as human and horse are both animals.
rows.anchor: الدلوك عبارة عن الميل والتغير وهذا المعنى حاصل في الغروب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some derive dulūk from rubbing the eyes while looking at the sun and thus restrict it to sunset; al-Rāzī replies that glare makes eye-rubbing more necessary at midday, favoring the sun’s decline.
rows.anchor: ومنهم من احتج أيضا على صحة هذا القول بأن الدلوك اشتقاقه من الدلك

rows.speaker: الواحدي
rows.claim: Al-Wāḥidī takes the lām in li-dulūk as causal: prayer becomes due at the sun’s decline, so it is performed on account of that decline.
rows.anchor: قال الواحدي : اللام في قوله لدلوك الشمس

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisāʾī glosses ghassaq al-layl as the night’s darkness and says ghassaaq is the noun with fatḥa on the sīn.
rows.anchor: قال الكسائي : غسق الليل غسوقا

rows.speaker: النضر بن شميل
rows.claim: Al-Naḍr ibn Shumayl defines ghassaq as the onset of night, when darkness mixes and obscures the view; al-Rāzī traces the root to flowing, as with tears or blood.
rows.anchor: وقال النضر بن شميل : غسق الليل دخول أوله

rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: In Ibn Jurayj’s report, ʿAṭāʾ says ghassaq is the beginning of night as it enters.
rows.anchor: قال ابن جريج : قلت لعطاء : ما غسق الليل

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās defines ghassaq as night entering with its darkness, in response to Nāfiʿ ibn al-Azraq.
rows.anchor: وسأل نافع بن الأزرق ابن عباس ما الغسق : قال دخول الليل بظلمته

rows.speaker: الأزهري
rows.claim: Al-Azharī places ghassaq at the disappearance of twilight, when darkness gathers and intensifies; he compares it to an eye full of tears or a wound full of blood.
rows.anchor: وقال الأزهري : غسق الليل عند غيبوبة الشفق عند تراكم الظلمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī prefers accumulated darkness at twilight’s disappearance: this interpretation includes all four prayers in the interval, whereas onset darkness would include only ẓuhr and maghrib.
rows.anchor: دخلت الصلوات الأربع فيه وهي الظهر والعصر والمغرب والعشاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If ghassaq is the first darkness, the verse names noon, first maghrib, and dawn, making noon shared by ẓuhr and ʿaṣr and first night shared by maghrib and ʿishāʾ; combining is then allowed for travel, rain, and similar excuses, not without excuse at home.
rows.anchor: هذا يقتضي جواز الجمع بين الظهر والعصر وبين المغرب والعشاء مطلقا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If ghassaq is accumulated darkness at the disappearance of white twilight, the endpoint leaves prayer lawful before then; this fits the view that the prayers become due at red twilight.
rows.anchor: الظلمة المتراكمة إنما تحصل عند غيبوبة الشفق الأبيض وكلمة إلى لانتهاء الغاية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commentators agree that Qurʾān al-fajr means the dawn prayer; it is coordinated with al-ṣalāh, with the sense, establish prayer and establish the dawn recitation.
rows.anchor: أجمعوا على أن المراد منه صلاة الصبح وانتصابه بالعطف على الصلاة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording shows that prayer is not complete without recitation.
rows.anchor: هذه الآية تدل على أن الصلاة لا تتم إلا بالقراءة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the command attaches recitation to dawn’s first appearance, obligation would seem to begin then; consensus removes obligation, leaving preference, so al-Rāzī says the verse supports al-Shāfiʿī’s view that praying at first light (taghlīs) is better than waiting for brightening.
rows.anchor: هذا يدل على صحة مذهب الشافعي في أن التغليس أفضل من التنوير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jurists hold that dawn prayer should have a longer recitation than other prayers; singling out Qurʾān at dawn marks the feature as especially complete and desirable.
rows.anchor: السنة أن تكون القراءة في هذه الصلاة أطول من القراءة في سائر الصلوات

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority say dawn prayer is witnessed because night and day angels gather behind the imam; day angels arrive during prayer, and after it night angels ascend reporting the worshippers and God’s forgiveness.
rows.anchor: قال الجمهور : معناه أن ملائكة الليل وملائكة النهار يجتمعون في صلاة الصبح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This angelic gathering supports taghlīs: night angels remain in the darkness at the prayer’s start, day angels arrive as its extended recitation brings daylight, so both witness it.
rows.anchor: هذا أيضا دليل قوي في أن التغليس أفضل من التنوير لأن الإنسان إذا شرع فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reading of witnessed dawn prayer is that the change from darkness to light displays God’s power; contemplating the world’s transition from death and stillness to life and motion during prayer illuminates knowledge and certainty.
rows.anchor: كلية هذا العالم من الظلمة إلى الضوء ومن الموت إلى الحياة ومن السكون إلى الحركة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This spiritual interpretation depends on beginning at taghlīs, when the transformation can be observed during the prayer.
rows.anchor: هذا الاعتبار لا يحصل إلا عند أداء صلاة الفجر على سبيل التغليس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third interpretation is witnessing through a large congregation: dawn prayer purifies hearts especially strongly, and worshippers reflect one another’s knowledge of God like facing mirrors reflecting sunlight, bringing spaciousness and comfort.
rows.anchor: كونه مشهودا بالجماعة الكثيرة ومزيد التحقيق فيه أنا بينا أن تأثير هذه الصلاة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sleep clears the mind’s tablet of worldly impressions; rising straight into worship and recitation inscribes sacred thoughts that prevent corrupt worldly desires from taking hold, so the benefit requires prayer at first light.
rows.anchor: صارت ألواح عقله وفكره وخياله مطهرة عن النقوش الفاسدة الباطلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because love of the world, greed, envy, and rivalry are diseases of hearts, prophets act like skilled physicians; beginning obedience on waking helps reduce this hard-to-cure illness and is therefore prescribed.
rows.anchor: مرض حب الدنيا مستول على الخلق ولا علاج له إلا بالدعوة إلى معرفة الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tahajjud is night prayer, and bi-hi means with the Qurʾān, namely prayer containing Qurʾānic recitation; al-Rāzī links this to the night-standing and measured-recitation commands in al-Muzzammil.
rows.anchor: التهجد عبارة عن صلاة الليل فقوله فتهجد به أي بالقرآن

rows.speaker: الواحدي
rows.claim: Al-Wāḥidī says the basic lexical meaning of hajūd is sleep; al-Rāzī cites Labīd’s line “We slept, for the night journey had grown long” as evidence.
rows.anchor: قال الواحدي الهجود في اللغة النوم وهو معروف كثير في الشعر

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda allows hājid to mean either a sleeper or someone praying at night.
rows.anchor: عن أبي عبيدة الهاجد النائم والهاجد المصلي بالليل

rows.speaker: ابن الأعرابي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Aʿrābī likewise uses hajada both for sleeping at night and for praying at night, making the word one of the opposites.
rows.anchor: وروى ثعلب عن ابن الأعرابي مثل هذا القول كأنه قال هجد الرجل

rows.speaker: الأزهري
rows.claim: Al-Azharī mediates: ordinary Arabic calls the sleeper hājid, while religious usage calls someone who rises from sleep to pray a mutahajid.
rows.anchor: المعروف في كلام العرب أن الهاجد هو النائم ثم رأينا أن في الشرع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī offers another derivation: the worshipper is called mutahajid because he casts sleep off himself, like a devout person called mutahannith for casting sin off.
rows.anchor: سمي متهجدا لالقائه الهجود عن نفسه كما قيل للعابد متحنث لألقائه الحنث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He also suggests the worshipper gives up sleep’s pleasure to attain the more delightful rest at death; because night prayer seeks that future rest, it may be called tahajjud.
rows.anchor: كان غرضه من ترك هذا الهجود أن يصل إلى الهجود اللذيذ عند الموت

rows.speaker: الحجاج بن عمرو المازني
rows.claim: Al-Ḥajjāj ibn ʿAmr al-Māzinī says tahajjud is prayer after sleeping, then another prayer after a later sleep and again after another nap; this was the Prophet’s practice.
rows.anchor: ما روي أن الحجاج بن عمرو المازني قال : أيحسب أحدكم إذا قام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since every prayer seeks subsequent rest and sleep, al-Rāzī says this could also explain the name tahajjud.
rows.anchor: كلما صلى الإنسان طلب هجودا ورقادا فلا يبعد أنه سمي تهجدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The syntax supplies an omitted command, “rise during part of the night,” to govern min and precede the fa; bi-hi means the Qurʾān, hence prayer that includes recitation.
rows.anchor: التقدير قم من الليل أي في بعض الليل فتهجد به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nafila means an addition beyond the original obligation, as in the discussion of spoils in 8:1.
rows.anchor: معنى النافلة في اللغة ما كان زيادة على الأصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view says night prayer was initially obligatory for the Prophet, then abrogated and made voluntary, an addition to the obligatory prayers.
rows.anchor: من الناس من قال إنها كانت واجبة عليه ثم نسخت فصارت نافلة

rows.speaker: مجاهد والسدي
rows.claim: Mujāhid and al-Suddī offer a good explanation: since God forgave the Prophet’s past and future sins, his extra worship adds rank and reward, whereas the community needs such worship to expiate sins; it is an addition specifically for him.
rows.anchor: وذكر مجاهد والسدي في تفسير كونها ( نافلة ) وجها حسنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who consider night prayer obligatory for the Prophet say nafila laka means a duty added to the five prayers specifically for him; the imperative supports obligation, avoiding conflict with a non-obligatory reading of nafila.
rows.anchor: أمر وصيغة الأمر للوجوب فوجب كون هذا التهجد واجبا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the five-prayer command is addressed to the Messenger, it applies to the community: the following night-prayer command is expressly restricted to him, so the unrestricted command cannot be Prophet-only.
rows.anchor: فبين أن الأمر بالتهجد مخصوص بالرسول وهذا يدل على أن الأمر بالصلاة الخمس

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: The commentators agree that when God says ʿasā, the promised outcome is certain: ʿasā expresses hope, and it would be disgraceful to raise hope then withhold the promise; God is too generous for that.
rows.anchor: اتفق المفسرون على أن كلمة عسى من الله واجب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Maḥmūdan can be parsed either as a circumstantial accusative from yabʿathuka, meaning He raises you praised, or as an adjective of maqām, which is the more apparent construction.
rows.anchor: في انتصاب قوله محمودا وجهان . الأول : أن يكون انتصابه

rows.speaker: الواحدي
rows.claim: Al-Wāḥidī says the commentators agree that the praised station is intercession, citing the Prophet’s explanation that he will intercede for his community there.
rows.anchor: قال الواحدي أجمع المفسرون على أنه مقام الشفاعة

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet explains this verse as the station where he intercedes for his community.
rows.anchor: قال النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم في هذه الآية ( هو المقام الذي أشفع فيه لأمتي )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī argues that praise follows a benefaction, and the promised future station cannot mean preaching already completed; it must be a later benefit the Prophet gives people, namely intercession.
rows.anchor: ذلك الإنعام لا يجوز أن يكون هو تبليغ الدين وتعليم الشرع لأن ذلك كان حاصلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The absolute, indefinite praised station implies immense praise, and rescuing people from punishment merits greater gratitude than adding reward to those who do not need it; this supports intercession for removal of punishment.
rows.anchor: حمد الإنسان على سعيه في التخليص عن العقاب أعظم من حمده في السعي في زيادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Authentic reports and the well-known supplication asking for the promised praised station confirm intercession; al-Rāzī says people agree that the supplication means intercession.
rows.anchor: ثم وردت الأخبار الصحيحة في تقرير هذا المعنى وجب حل اللفظ عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The familiar supplication asks God to raise the Prophet to the promised praised station, which al-Rāzī says everyone understands as intercession.
rows.anchor: واتفق الناس على أن المراد منه الشفاعة

rows.speaker: حذيفة
rows.claim: Ḥudhayfa describes the gathering on a plain where none can speak, with Muhammad first called and answering with a prayer of submission; this is offered as the praised station.
rows.anchor: قال حذيفة ، يجمع الناس في صعيد فلا تتكلم نفس فأول مدعو محمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī prefers intercession: the reported prayer earns reward but does not itself make people praise the Prophet; if God’s praise is proposed, ordinary Arabic praise is for benefaction, so that reading is figurative.
rows.anchor: وأقول القول الأول أولى لأن سعيه في الشفاعة يفيده إقدام الناس على حمده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The third proposal, a station whose outcome is praised, is weak for the same reason: it does not explain the benefaction that makes the Prophet praised.
rows.anchor: للوجه الذي ذكرناه في القول الثاني

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود ومجاهد
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd says God seats Muhammad on the Throne, while Mujāhid says He seats him with Him there; al-Wāḥidī calls the report abhorrent and appalling.
rows.anchor: قال الواحدي روى عن ابن مسعود أنه قال : ( يقعد الله محمدا على العرش ) وعن مجاهد أنه قال يجلسه معه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The throne reading reverses the ordinary meaning of baʿatha, “to send,” and confuses maqām, a standing place, with a seat; neither word means seating someone beside God.
rows.anchor: أن البعث ضد الإجلاس يقال بعثت النازل والقاعد فانبعث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Seating Muhammad beside God on the Throne would make God bounded and finite, and therefore created.
rows.anchor: لكان محدودا متناهيا ومن كان كذلك فهو محدث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The proposed seating offers no distinct honor if, as its proponents say, all believers in Paradise visit God, sit with Him, and speak with Him.
rows.anchor: إذا كانت هذه الحالة حاصلة عندهم لكل المؤمنين لم يكن لتخصيص محمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In ordinary usage, saying a ruler raised or sent someone means he dispatched him to manage people’s affairs, not that he seated him beside himself.
rows.anchor: فهم منه أنه أرسله إلى قوم لإصلاح مهماتهم ولا يفهم منه أنه أجلسه مع نفسه

rows.speaker: الحسن وقتادة
rows.claim: If 17:76 concerns Meccan pagans trying to expel the Prophet, al-Ḥasan and Qatāda read the prayer as asking to enter Medina in truthful migration and leave Mecca truthfully.
rows.anchor: وهذا قول الحسن وقتادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If 17:76 instead concerns Jews urging the Prophet to leave Medina for Syria, the prayer on his return asks to re-enter Medina truthfully and to leave for Mecca through a truthful conquest.
rows.anchor: عند العود إلى المدينة قال : { رب أدخلنى مدخل صدق } وهو المدينة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A more complete spiritual reading asks God to admit the Prophet into prayer with sincerity and devotion, and let him leave it with sincerity, remembrance, and gratitude.
rows.anchor: والقول الثاني : في تفسير هذه الآية وهو أكمل مما سبق أن المراد { وقل رب أدخلنى } في الصلاة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further reading asks to enter prayer and leave it with no remaining liability or blame.
rows.anchor: منها بعد الفراغ منها إخراجا لا يبقى علي منها تبعة ربقية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A higher mystical reading asks to enter the seas of proofs for divine unity and transcendence, then pass from reasoning about created effects to direct knowledge of the singular, changeless God.
rows.anchor: في بحار دلائل توحيدك وتنزيهك وقدسك ثم أخرجني من الاشتغال بالدليل إلى ضياء معرفة المدلول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reading asks to enter and leave every situation with truthful servitude, knowledge, love, and worship, so sincerity marks every movement and stillness.
rows.anchor: أدخلني في كل ما تدخلني فيه مع الصدق في عبوديتك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A final interpretation asks for a truthful entrance into the grave and a truthful exit from it.
rows.anchor: أدخلني القبر مدخل صدق وأخرجني منه مخرج صدق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Madkhal with ḍamma on the mīm is a verbal noun like idkhāl; al-Rāzī compares the construction with the prayer for a blessed landing in 23:29.
rows.anchor: مدخل بضم الميم مصدر كالإدخال يقال أدخلته مدخلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adding “truth” to entrance and exit praises them: the supplicant asks for good entries and departures in which nothing disliked occurs.
rows.anchor: ومعنى إضافة المدخل والمخرج إلى الصدق مدحهما كأنه سأل الله تعالى إدخالا حسنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A helping authority means a clear proof with which God enables the Prophet to overcome every opponent; the request also includes power and ability.
rows.anchor: أي حجة بينة ظاهرة تنصرني بها على جميع من خالفني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God answers the plea for protection and victory in other verses, including the promise to protect the Messenger, the triumph of God’s party, and the promise to make His religion prevail.
rows.anchor: فقال : { والله يعصمك من الناس } ( المائدة : 67 ) وقال : { ألا إن حزب الله هم المفلحون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The truth that has come is the Prophet’s religion and law, while falsehood is every other religion and law; zahāqa means to perish and disappear, from the expression for a soul that perishes.
rows.anchor: وهو دينه وشرعه { وزهق الباطل } وهو كل ما سواه من الأديان والشرائع

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd entered Mecca at the conquest when 360 idols surrounded the Kaʿba, struck them with a stick while reciting the verse, and each idol fell face-first.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن مسعود : ( أنه دخل مكة يوم الفتح وحول البيت ثلاثمائة وستون صنما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Falsehood may temporarily enjoy rule and force, but its authority cannot last and disappears swiftly.
rows.anchor: يعني أن الباطل وإن اتفقت له دولة وصولة إلا أنها الا تبقى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After explaining theology, prophecy, resurrection, divine decree, and prayer’s secrets through the Qurʾān, God clarifies that the Qurʾān is healing and mercy.
rows.anchor: لما أطنب في شرح الإلهيات والنبوات والحشر والمعاد والبعث وإثبات القضاء والقدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Min is generic, not partitive, as in the command to avoid the abomination of idols; the whole Qurʾān is healing for believers.
rows.anchor: ليست للتبعيض بل هي للجنس كقوله : { فاجتنبوا الرجس من الاوثان }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qurʾān cures spiritual disease from false beliefs: it proves truth about God, prophecy, resurrection, and decree while exposing errors in rival doctrines.
rows.anchor: أشدها فسادا الاعتقادات الفاسدة في الإلهيات والنبوات والمعاد والقضاء والقدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It also cures moral disease by explaining the harm in blameworthy traits and guiding people toward virtuous character and praiseworthy deeds.
rows.anchor: القرآن مشتمل على تفصيلها وتعريف ما فيها من المفاسد والإرشاد إلى الأخلاق الفاضلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qurʾān can also heal bodily illness: blessing from its recitation wards off many diseases.
rows.anchor: التبرك بقراءته يدفع كثيرا من الأمراض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even philosophers and talisman practitioners acknowledge effects from incomprehensible charms; a fortiori, reciting the Qurʾān, which glorifies God and the angels and disparages devils, should bring religious and worldly benefit; al-Rāzī also cites a prophetic healing report.
rows.anchor: فلأن تكون قراءة هذا القرآن العظيم المشتمل على ذكر الله وكبريائه وتعظيم الملائكة

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī quotes the Prophet as saying that whoever does not seek healing through the Qurʾān will not be healed by God.
rows.anchor: بما روى أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال : ( من لم يستشف بالقرآن فلا شفاه الله تعالى )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qurʾān is mercy through teaching high knowledge and virtuous character, by which a person approaches the Lord and joins the company of the angels; healing removes illness, while mercy cultivates health, so healing comes first.
rows.anchor: إزالة المرض مقدمة على السعي في تكميل موجبات الصحة لا جرم بدأ الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For wrongdoers, identified here as polytheists, hearing the Qurʾān intensifies anger, rancor, and envy; these traits drive corrupt deeds that reinforce them, deepening disgrace and error.
rows.anchor: سماع القرآن يزيدهم غيظا وغضبا وحقدا وحسدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī identifies love of worldly life, desire for wealth and status, and the belief that effort secures them as the underlying cause of the wrongdoers’ continuing loss.
rows.anchor: ذكر السبب الأصلي في وقوع هؤلا الجاهلين الضالين في أودية الضلال ومقامات الخزي

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās identifies “the human” as al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra; al-Rāzī calls this interpretation far-fetched.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما : إن الإنسان ها هنا هو الوليد بن المغيرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī instead reads the verse generally: people tend to become arrogant, forget servitude, and rebel against God when they obtain what they want, as 96:6–7 says.
rows.anchor: المراد أن نوع الإنسان من شأنه أنه إذا فاز بمقصوده ووصل إلى مطلوبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aʿraḍa means he turned away, literally turning his face aside; naʾā bi-jānibihi means he moved far away.
rows.anchor: قوله أعرض أي ولى ظهره أي عرضه إلى ناحية ونأى بجانبه أي تباعد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moving one’s flank away is an idiom for arrogance, since the arrogant customarily turn aside and present their backs.
rows.anchor: والنأي بالجانب أن يلوي عنه عطفه ويوليه ظهره وأراد الاستكبار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The common reading has fatḥa on both nūn and hamza in naʾā; it is the dominant Arabic form and also occurs in Sūrat Ḥā Mīm al-Sajda.
rows.anchor: قراءة العامة بفتح النون والهمزة وفي حم السجدة مثله

rows.speaker: ابن عامر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀmir reads nāʾ; it can reflect metathesis of the word’s final and middle radicals, as in rāʾ for raʾā, or derive from a verb meaning to rise.
rows.anchor: قراءة ابن عامر ناء وله وجهان تقديم اللام على العين كقولهم راء في رأى

rows.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī incline both fatḥas: they incline the hamza and then give the nūn kasra by assimilation to that vowel.
rows.anchor: قراءة حمزة والكسائي بإمالة الفتحتين وذلك لأنهم أمالوا الهمزة من نأى

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو وعاصم وحمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr, ʿĀṣim in Abū Bakr’s narration, and Naṣīr from al-Kisāʾī and Ḥamza read naʾā with an open nūn and kasra on the hamza, inclining the hamza.
rows.anchor: قرأ أبو عمرو وعاصم في رواية أبي بكر ونصير عن الكسائي وحمزة نأى بفتح النون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The evil that touches a person includes poverty, sickness, or any calamity; then he is intensely despairing of God’s mercy.
rows.anchor: إذا مسه فقر أو مرض أو نازلة من النوازل كان يؤوسا شديد اليأس من رحمة الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The person who prospers forgets God, while the deprived person is consumed by grief and also fails to remember God; al-Rāzī compares the pattern with 89:15–16 and 70:19–21.
rows.anchor: إن فاز بالنعمة والدولة اغتر بها فنسي ذكر الله ، وإن بقي في الحرمان عن الدنيا

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj glosses shākila as a path or doctrine, supported by the expression for a road with many branches.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج : الشاكلة الطريقة والمذهب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation is that each person acts according to the nature of the soul: a luminous, pure, higher soul produces noble deeds, and a murky, base soul produces corrupt ones.
rows.anchor: كل أحد يفعل على وفق ما شاكل جوهر نفسه ومقتضى روحه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Philosophers disagree whether human souls differ essentially or are essentially equal, with differing temperaments causing their actions; al-Rāzī prefers essential difference, which fits the preceding contrast in how souls respond to the Qurʾān and the sun’s opposite effects on salt, fat, and a launderer.
rows.anchor: المختار عندي هو القسم الأول والقرآن مشعر بذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question about the spirit follows the claim that each person acts according to the pattern of the soul; the discussion therefore turns to the spirit’s nature.
rows.anchor: وجب البحث ها هنا عن ماهية الروح وحقيقته فلذلك سألوا عن الروح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The most apparent interpretation is the life-giving human spirit; al-Rāzī recounts the report that Jews told Quraysh to ask about the Cave Companions, Dhul-Qarnayn, and the spirit.
rows.anchor: أظهرها أن المراد منه الروح الذي هو سبب الحياة ، روى أن اليهود قالوا لقريش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the report, the Prophet promised an answer the next day without saying “if God wills”; revelation then ceased for forty days before the exception in 18:23–24 was revealed.
rows.anchor: ولم يقل إن شاء / الله فانقطع عنه الوحي أربعين يوما ثم نزل الوحي بعده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The same report says he later related the Cave and Dhul-Qarnayn stories but left the spirit question ambiguous, prompting this verse.
rows.anchor: ثم فسر لهم قصة أصحاب الكهف وقصة ذي القرنين وأبهم قصة الروح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī objects that the spirit is not greater or higher than God; since knowledge of God is possible, there is no apparent barrier to knowing the spirit.
rows.anchor: أن الروح ليس أعظم شأنا ولا أعلى مكانا من الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He objects that answering stories about the Cave and Dhul-Qarnayn cannot prove prophethood: before belief, Quraysh could simply disbelieve the stories; after belief, the stories add nothing, and silence about the spirit is no proof either.
rows.anchor: قصة أصحاب الكهف وقصة ذي القرنين ليست إلا حكاية من الحكايات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If even junior philosophers and low-ranking speculative theologians know about the spirit, a Prophet’s professed ignorance would invite contempt and repel people.
rows.anchor: مسألة الروح يعرفها أصاغر الفلاسفة وأراذل المتكلمين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qurʾān says God taught the Prophet the Book and what he did not know, commands him to seek more knowledge, and says all things are recorded; the Prophet prayed to see things as they are, so al-Rāzī asks how he could lack this knowledge.
rows.anchor: وعلمك ما لم تكن تعلم وكان فضل الله عليك عظيما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī’s preferred answer is that ruh can prompt many questions—about substance, spatiality, eternity, survival after death, or the soul’s happiness and misery—and the verse does not specify which one was asked.
rows.anchor: ليس فيه ما يدل على أنهم عن هذه المسائل سألوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reply that the spirit is from God’s command suits questions about its essence or whether it is originated; al-Rāzī says these are the two issues to which the answer applies.
rows.anchor: وهذا الجواب لا يليق إلا بمسألتين من المسائل التي ذكرناها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For the question about essence, al-Rāzī says the spirit is distinct from bodies and accidents: it is a simple, immaterial substance, brought into being by God’s creative “Be.”
rows.anchor: بل هو جوهر بسيط مجرد لا يحدث إلا بمحدث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The spirit is created by God’s command and gives life to the body; ignorance of its particular reality does not negate it, since many realities are unknown.
rows.anchor: موجود يحدث بأمر الله وتكوينه وتأثيره في إفادة الحياة لهذا الجسد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī illustrates with sikangabīn: people know it cuts yellow bile, though the specific reality of that property remains unknown, so ignorance does not prove nonexistence.
rows.anchor: نعلم أن السكنجبين له خاصية تقتضي قطع الصفراء فأما إذا أردنا أن نعرف ماهية تلك الخاصية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Amr can mean an act, as in the Qurʾānic descriptions of Pharaoh’s conduct and God’s deed in 11:97 and 11:66.
rows.anchor: لفظ الأمر قد جاء بمعنى الفعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On this reading, “the spirit is from my Lord’s act” answers whether the spirit is eternal or originated: it is originated through God’s creation and bringing it into being.
rows.anchor: أي من فعل ربي وهذا الجواب يدل على أنهم سألوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The spirit begins without knowledge, then gains knowledge and changes from one state to another; this change indicates origination, which al-Rāzī takes as the force of the verse’s statement that people received little knowledge.
rows.anchor: الأرواح في مبدأ الفطرة تكون خالية عن العلوم والمعارف ثم يحصل فيها العلوم والمعارف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view identifies the spirit as the Qurʾān, which God calls a spirit in 42:52 and 16:2 because it gives life to souls and minds through knowledge of God, angels, scripture, and messengers.
rows.anchor: أن المراد من هذا الروح هو القرآن قالوا وذلك لأن الله تعالى سمى القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qurʾān reading fits the context: 17:82 and 17:86–88 discuss the Qurʾān, and the questioners may have asked whether it was poetry or soothsaying; the answer says it is divine revelation, not human speech.
rows.anchor: فلما كان قبل هذه الآية في وصف القرآن وما بعدها كذلك وجب أيضا أن يكون المراد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view identifies the spirit with the greatest of the heavenly angels, citing the spirit standing with the angels in 78:38.
rows.anchor: الروح المسؤول عنه في هذه الآية ملك من ملائكة السموات وهو أعظمهم قدرا وقوة

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
rows.claim: A report attributed to ʿAlī describes this angel as having 70,000 faces, each with 70,000 further faces and tongues and languages praising God; each praise creates an angel, and no creation is greater except the Throne.
rows.anchor: عن علي بن أبي طالب رضي الله عنه أنه قال : هو ملك له سبعون ألف وجه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī objects that if ʿAlī knew this description, the Prophet should have known it too; ʿAlī could only have learned it from the Prophet, so it is unclear why the Prophet would tell him and not others.
rows.anchor: هذا التفصيل لما عرفه علي ، فالنبي أولى أن يكون قد عرفه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The multiplied languages serve no purpose if one creature speaks them all; if a different creature speaks each language, the account describes many angels rather than one.
rows.anchor: إن كان حيوانا واحدا وعاقلا واحدا لم يكن في تكثير تلك اللغات فائدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī says the immense angel is an unknown being, an unlikely subject of inquiry; the familiar life-giving human spirit is the likelier referent.
rows.anchor: أما الروح الذي هو سبب الحياة فهو شيء تتوفر دواعي العقلاء على معرفته

rows.speaker: الحسن وقتادة
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan and Qatāda identify the spirit as Gabriel, whom God calls the trustworthy spirit and “Our spirit”; Gabriel says that he descends only by his Lord’s command.
rows.anchor: وهو قول الحسن وقتادة أن هذا الروح جبريل والدليل عليه أنه تعالى سمى جبريل

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says the spirit is a creation outside the angels, resembling human beings and having hands, feet, heads, and the ability to eat.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد : الروح خلق ليسوا من الملائكة على صورة بني آدم يأكلون

rows.speaker: أبو صالح
rows.claim: Abū Ṣāliḥ says these beings resemble people but are not people; al-Rāzī finds no Qurʾānic or sound-report evidence for this unknown interpretation and considers it an unlikely question.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو صالح يشبهون الناس وليسوا بالناس ولم أجد في القرآن ولا في الأخبار الصحيحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī starts from certain self-awareness: when a person says “I” while knowing, thinking, seeing, hearing, or feeling, what is that self—body, accident, their combination, something distinct, or a combination with that third thing?
rows.anchor: العلم الضروري حاصل بأن ها هنا شيئا إليه يشير الإنسان بقوله أنا

rows.speaker: جمهور المتكلمين
rows.claim: Most speculative theologians identify the human with the visible bodily structure and say no formal definition is needed; al-Rāzī rejects this identification.
rows.anchor: القائلون بأن الإنسان عبارة عن هذه البنية المحسوسة وعن هذا الجسم المحسوس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The body’s parts change through growth, aging, weight gain, and loss, while the enduring self remains; since change differs from what persists, the person is not the sum of the body.
rows.anchor: أجزاء هذه الجثة متبدلة بالزيادة والنقصان تارة بحسب النمو والذبول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When focused on one matter, a person may be unaware of every body part yet remain aware of self and say “I was angry” or “I heard”; the self therefore differs from the body and its parts.
rows.anchor: فهو في تلك الحالة عالم بنفسه المخصوصة وغافل عن جملة بدنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People call body parts “my head,” “my eye,” and “my hand”; the owner is distinct from what is owned, so the human differs from the body and its parts.
rows.anchor: كل أحد يحكم عقله بإضافة كل واحد من هذه الأعضاء إلى نفسه فيقول رأسي وعيني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The objection that saying “my self” makes the person distinct from himself is answered by distinguishing the body, which is other than the human essence, from the specific reality meant by “I,” which cannot be re-added to itself.
rows.anchor: فإذا قال نفسي وذاتي فإن كان المراد البدن فعندنا أنه مغاير لجوهر الإنسان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Any proof that a human cannot be a body also shows that the human cannot be identified with this particular body; al-Rāzī says he will detail such proofs later.
rows.anchor: كل دليل على أن الإنسان يمتنع أن يكون جسما فهو أيضا يدل على أنه يمتنع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A person remains alive when the body is dead: the Qurʾān calls slain martyrs alive with their Lord, while the senses show their bodies are dead, so the person differs from the body.
rows.anchor: ولا تحسبن الذين قتلوا في سبيل الله أمواتا بل أحياء عند ربهم يرزقون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurʾānic descriptions of the dead exposed to Fire and of those drowned entering Fire, along with reports that prophets move between abodes, graves are gardens or pits, and death begins one’s Hour, show the person survives the dead body; identifying that person with a living corpse would make every inanimate thing potentially alive.
rows.anchor: النار يعرضون عليها غدوا وعشيا

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: A long sermon attributed to the Prophet says the dead person’s spirit hovers over the bier, warns family not to be deceived by worldly life, and laments that wealth gathered lawfully and unlawfully goes to others while the liability remains with him.
rows.anchor: قوله عليه السلام في خطبة طويلة له ( حتى إذا حمل الميت على نعشه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī infers that the person is still alive and aware while the body lies dead on the bier, proving that the human differs from the body.
rows.anchor: كان ذلك الإنسان حيا باقيا فاهما وذلك تصريح بأن الإنسان شيء مغاير لهذا الجسد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to the tranquil soul to return to its Lord addresses it at death and describes it as content and accepted; the surviving, living soul is the human, distinct from the dead body.
rows.anchor: ارجعى إلى ربك راضية مرضية } ( الفجر : 27 ، 28 ) والخطاب بقوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At death, the messengers take a person and the dead are returned to God, their true Master; because the body is dead, the one returned must differ from it.
rows.anchor: توفته رسلنا وهم لا يفرطون * ثم ردوا إلى الله مولاهم الحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People across nations and religions give charity for their dead, pray for them, and visit their graves; these practices would be pointless unless the person survived the body, which al-Rāzī says accords with sound original human nature.
rows.anchor: يتصدقون عن موتاهم ويدعون لهم بالخير ويذهبون إلى زياراتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Many people dream that a deceased parent or child reveals hidden treasure or requests repayment of a debt, then find the information correct; al-Rāzī takes this as evidence the person survives bodily death.
rows.anchor: كثيرا من الناس يرى أباه أو ابنه بعد موته في المنام ويقول له اذهب إلى الموضع الفلاني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If hands, legs, eyes, or ears are lost, a person still experiences himself as the same person as before; this proves the self differs from those body parts and refutes identifying the human with the bodily structure.
rows.anchor: فإن ذلك الإنسان يجد من قلبه وعقله أنه هو عين ذلك الإنسان
